title: Antipsychotics and extrapyramidal side effects
blurb: Recognise extrapyramidal and other antipsychotic side effects, act on them, and follow the NICE physical health monitoring schedule.
question: Danny, 19, started haloperidol yesterday for first-episode psychosis. This morning his neck is twisted to one side, his eyes are rolling upwards and he is frightened. What is happening and what should the nurse do?

teach.h: How antipsychotics work, and why side effects follow
teach.body: Antipsychotics reduce psychotic symptoms mainly by blocking dopamine D2 receptors. First-generation (typical) drugs, such as haloperidol, act mostly there and more often cause extrapyramidal side effects (EPSE) and raised prolactin. Second-generation (atypical) drugs, such as olanzapine or aripiprazole, act on more receptors: generally fewer EPSE, but more weight gain and glucose problems. In plain English: blocking dopamine calms psychosis but can upset movement, hormones and metabolism.
teach.cite: BNF treatment summary: psychoses and related disorders

teach.caption: Risperidone and amisulpride also commonly raise prolactin; aripiprazole lowers it.

teach.h: Extrapyramidal side effects: when they appear

items.label: Acute dystonia: muscle spasm, oculogyric crisis
Tardive dyskinesia: lip, tongue, jaw movements

teach.caption: Dystonia is more common in young men; parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia in older women (BNF).

teach.h: Other side effects to ask about

teach.body: Danny has an acute dystonic reaction: sustained neck spasm and an oculogyric crisis, within a day of starting a first-generation drug, in a young man. Nurse Patel stays with him, reassures him, checks his airway and breathing, and contacts the prescriber urgently; an antimuscarinic such as procyclidine can relieve it. She records the reaction, withholds the next haloperidol dose pending review, and explains to Danny what happened so he does not stop treatment in fear.

teach.h: Good practice in prescribing and giving
items: Treat each antipsychotic as a therapeutic trial: start low, titrate, optimum dose for 4-6 weeks (CG178 1.3.6.3).
Avoid high or rapidly escalating doses for acute psychosis ('rapid neuroleptisation', CG178 1.3.6.9).
Avoid combining antipsychotics except briefly when switching (CG178 1.3.6.10).
Check PRN does not push the total above the BNF maximum (CG178 1.3.6.8).
Typicals: more EPSE and prolactin; atypicals: more weight gain and glucose problems.
EPSE order: dystonia (hours), akathisia (hours-weeks), parkinsonism (gradual), tardive dyskinesia (long-term).
Akathisia can be mistaken for agitation; tardive dyskinesia is not helped by antimuscarinics.
Monitor weight weekly for 6 weeks; BP, glucose/HbA1c and lipids at 12 weeks, 1 year, then yearly.

summary: You can now distinguish typical and atypical antipsychotics, recognise each extrapyramidal side effect by its timing and features, and respond safely. You can also apply the NICE CG178 physical health monitoring schedule.

A.q: Which extrapyramidal side effect typically appears within hours of starting an antipsychotic, especially in young men?
A.why: BNF: acute dystonia can appear within hours of starting antipsychotics and is more common in young males.

whyNot.0: Tardive dyskinesia develops with long-term or high-dose treatment.
whyNot.1: Parkinsonism appears gradually and is more common in older women.
whyNot.3: Hyperprolactinaemia is a hormonal effect, not an extrapyramidal one.

A.q: Under NICE CG178, how often should weight be measured in the first 6 weeks after starting an antipsychotic?
A.why: CG178 1.3.6.4: weight weekly for the first 6 weeks, then at 12 weeks, at 1 year and annually.

whyNot.0: Daily weighing is not the CG178 schedule.
whyNot.2: Fortnightly is less often than CG178 recommends.
whyNot.3: A single check at 6 weeks misses rapid early weight gain.

A.q: Which antipsychotic side effect is NOT relieved by antimuscarinic drugs such as procyclidine?
A.why: BNF: tardive dyskinesia has no satisfactory treatment; antimuscarinics relieve parkinsonism and dystonia but not tardive dyskinesia.

whyNot.2: Rigidity from drug-induced parkinsonism can respond to antimuscarinics.

B.q: Two weeks after his antipsychotic dose was increased, Kieran, 30, paces constantly and says, 'I feel like I'm going to jump out of my skin.' Staff suggest PRN for agitation. What is the most likely explanation?
B.why: BNF: akathisia (restlessness) occurs within hours to weeks of starting or increasing an antipsychotic and may be mistaken for psychotic agitation.

whyNot.1: The timing after a dose increase and the inner restlessness point to akathisia, not relapse.
whyNot.2: Tardive dyskinesia causes involuntary facial movements, usually after long-term use.
whyNot.3: Serotonin syndrome follows serotonergic drugs and includes clonus, hyperthermia and confusion.

B.q: Grace, 26, takes risperidone and reports her periods have stopped and her breasts are leaking milk. Which side effect is most likely?
B.why: BNF: risperidone is among the drugs most likely to cause symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia, with menstrual disturbance and galactorrhoea.

whyNot.0: Dystonia is a muscle spasm, not a hormonal effect.
whyNot.1: NMS presents with fever, rigidity, altered consciousness and autonomic instability.
whyNot.2: Hypothyroidism is associated with lithium, not risperidone, and does not typically cause galactorrhoea.

B.q: Which baseline check does NICE CG178 list before starting an antipsychotic?
options: Fasting glucose or HbA1c and lipids
B.why: CG178 1.3.6.1: baseline weight, waist, pulse and BP, fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids, prolactin, movement disorders and nutrition and activity.

whyNot.0: These are lithium baseline tests, not antipsychotic baseline tests.
whyNot.1: These are not CG178 baseline investigations.
whyNot.3: These are not routine antipsychotic baseline tests.

C.q: Danny, 19, started haloperidol yesterday. His neck is twisted to one side and his eyes are fixed upwards. He is distressed but breathing normally. What should the nurse do first?
options: Give his next haloperidol dose to settle him
Reassure him and seek urgent prescriber review
Record it and review at the next ward round
Restrain him to stop him injuring his neck
C.why: This is acute dystonia with an oculogyric crisis. The nurse reassures him, monitors his airway and contacts the prescriber urgently; an antimuscarinic can relieve it, and the antipsychotic is reviewed.

whyNot.0: More haloperidol is likely to worsen the dystonia.
whyNot.2: Acute dystonia is distressing and can affect the airway; it needs prompt treatment.
whyNot.3: Restraint is not indicated for an involuntary muscle spasm.

C.q: Mrs Hughes, 68, has taken a first-generation antipsychotic for many years. Her daughter notices repetitive lip-smacking and tongue movements. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Increase the antipsychotic to mask it
Report it for a medication review
Reassure her daughter that it is a habit
C.why: These are features of tardive dyskinesia. Report for prescriber review; BNF advises regular review and gradual dose changes, and manufacturers suggest withdrawal at the earliest signs may halt its development.

whyNot.0: Antimuscarinics do not help tardive dyskinesia.
whyNot.1: Increasing the dose to mask it is not the safe response and risks further harm.
whyNot.3: Dismissing new involuntary movements delays review of a potentially irreversible effect.

C.q: Ben, 24, has taken olanzapine for 12 weeks. Which set of checks is due now under NICE CG178?
options: Weight, pulse, BP, glucose or HbA1c and lipids
Weight alone, as bloods are done at 1 year
Full blood count weekly for 18 weeks
C.why: CG178 1.3.6.4: at 12 weeks, check weight, pulse and blood pressure, fasting glucose or HbA1c and lipids; olanzapine commonly causes weight gain.

whyNot.1: Bloods are due at 12 weeks as well as at 1 year.
whyNot.2: Weekly FBC for 18 weeks is the clozapine schedule.

reteach.title: Movement, hormones, metabolism
reteach.question: How do you remember antipsychotic side effects?

blocks.body: Blocking dopamine affects movement (EPSE), hormones (prolactin) and, with many atypicals, metabolism (weight and glucose). For movement, remember the timeline: dystonia in hours, akathisia in hours to weeks, parkinsonism gradually, tardive dyskinesia after long-term use. Then follow the monitoring schedule so metabolic harm is caught early.

blocks.text: Restless pacing after a dose increase may be akathisia, not relapse.

explain.body: First-generation drugs mainly block dopamine D2 receptors and more often cause EPSE and raised prolactin. Second-generation drugs act on more receptors, with generally fewer EPSE but more weight gain and glucose intolerance.

test.q: Which antipsychotic is a first-generation (typical) drug?
test.why: BNF lists haloperidol (a butyrophenone) among the first-generation antipsychotics.

explain.body: Acute dystonia (spasm, hours), akathisia (restlessness, hours to weeks), parkinsonism (tremor, slowness, gradual) and tardive dyskinesia (involuntary face and tongue movements, long-term, possibly irreversible).

test.q: A man on long-term antipsychotics has involuntary chewing and tongue-thrusting movements. What is this?
test.why: Abnormal involuntary movements of lips, tongue, face and jaw on long-term treatment are tardive dyskinesia (BNF).

whyNot.0: Akathisia is subjective and motor restlessness.
whyNot.2: Acute dystonia is sustained spasm soon after starting.
whyNot.3: Parkinsonism causes tremor and slowness, not chewing movements.

explain.body: Dopamine normally inhibits prolactin, so most antipsychotics raise it: galactorrhoea, menstrual disturbance, sexual dysfunction. Cardiac effects include QT prolongation and postural hypotension; an ECG is offered if indicated.

test.q: Before starting an antipsychotic, when does NICE CG178 say an ECG should be offered?
options: Once the first dose has been given
When weight gain exceeds 7% at 12 weeks
test.why: CG178 1.3.6.2: offer an ECG if the SPC specifies, cardiovascular risk is found, there is a personal history of CVD, or the person is being admitted as an in-patient.

whyNot.0: CG178 does not require an ECG for every outpatient.
whyNot.2: The ECG is considered before starting, not after.
whyNot.3: Weight gain is not a CG178 ECG criterion.

explain.body: Baseline weight, waist, pulse, BP, glucose or HbA1c, lipids, prolactin and movement disorders. Then weight weekly for 6 weeks, at 12 weeks, 1 year and yearly; pulse, BP, glucose and lipids at 12 weeks, 1 year and yearly.

test.q: When are blood glucose (or HbA1c) and lipids next checked after the baseline, under NICE CG178?
test.why: CG178 1.3.6.4: fasting glucose or HbA1c and lipids at 12 weeks, at 1 year and then annually.

whyNot.0: Two weeks is not a CG178 checkpoint for bloods.
whyNot.1: Six weeks is the end of weekly weighing, not a blood test point.
whyNot.3: Six months is not in the CG178 schedule.
